```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(httr2)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10))

set.seed(664)  # Only matters if we add simulation or bootstrap steps.

start_date <- as.Date("2000-01-01")
end_date <- as.Date("2026-09-01")
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| include: false

# Same data pipeline as the plan (STOR_664_Project.qmd).
# Download the publicly available French data archives.

base_url <- paste0(
  "https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/",
  "faculty/ken.french/ftp/"
)

download_french <- function(filename) {
  destination <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")

  request(paste0(base_url, filename)) |>
    req_user_agent("Mozilla/5.0") |>
    req_perform(path = destination)

  extraction_dir <- tempfile()
  dir.create(extraction_dir)

  files <- unzip(destination, exdir = extraction_dir)

  csv_file <- files[
    grepl("\\.csv$", files, ignore.case = TRUE)
  ][1]

  readLines(csv_file, warn = FALSE)
}

# Extract the monthly table, excluding annual summaries.

read_monthly <- function(lines) {
  monthly <- grepl("^\\s*[0-9]{6}\\s*,", lines)

  first <- which(monthly)[1]
  last <- first

  while (last < length(lines) && monthly[last + 1]) {
    last <- last + 1
  }

  block <- lines[c(first - 1, first:last)]

  result <- read.csv(
    text = paste(block, collapse = "\n"),
    check.names = FALSE,
    strip.white = TRUE
  )

  names(result)[1] <- "ym"
  result$ym <- as.character(result$ym)

  result
}

industry_raw <- read_monthly(
  download_french("5_Industry_Portfolios_CSV.zip")
)

factors_raw <- read_monthly(
  download_french("F-F_Research_Data_Factors_CSV.zip")
)

# Retain monthly returns, reported in percentage points.

industry <- industry_raw |>
  select(ym, Cnsmr, Manuf, HiTec, Hlth, Other)

factors <- factors_raw |>
  select(ym, `Mkt-RF`, RF)

data <- inner_join(industry, factors, by = "ym") |>
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(paste0(ym, "01"), format = "%Y%m%d"),
    market = `Mkt-RF`,
    health = Hlth - RF,
    negative = as.integer(market < 0),
    interaction = market * negative
  ) |>
  filter(
    date >= start_date,
    date <= end_date,
    if_all(
      c(Cnsmr, Manuf, HiTec, Hlth, Other, market, RF),
      ~ is.finite(.x) & .x > -99
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(date)

n_negative <- sum(data$negative == 1)
n_nonnegative <- sum(data$negative == 0)

# TODO: If we pin the sample to a fixed end date for reproducibility
# (the French library updates monthly), add e.g.
#   end_date <- as.Date("2026-09-01")
# to the setup chunk and filter(date <= end_date) here.
```

```{r}
#| label: data-validation

# Automated data integrity checks (unchanged from the plan).
# Execution stops if any assertion fails.

stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(industry$ym),
  !anyDuplicated(factors$ym)
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(data) > 0,
  all(!is.na(data$date)),
  !anyDuplicated(data$date),
  all(data$date >= start_date),
  identical(data$date, sort(data$date))
)

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(data$market)),
  all(is.finite(data$health)),
  all(is.finite(data$RF))
)

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(data$health, data$Hlth - data$RF)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(data$market, data[["Mkt-RF"]]))
)

stopifnot(
  identical(data$negative, as.integer(data$market < 0)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(data$interaction, data$market * data$negative))
)

expected_months <- seq(
  from = min(data$date),
  to = max(data$date),
  by = "month"
)

stopifnot(identical(data$date, expected_months))
```

```{r}
#| label: main-models
#| include: false

# Primary models from the plan.

model_simple <- lm(health ~ market, data = data)

model_asymmetric <- lm(health ~ market + interaction, data = data)

beta_positive <- unname(coef(model_asymmetric)["market"])

beta_negative <- unname(
  coef(model_asymmetric)["market"] +
    coef(model_asymmetric)["interaction"]
)

slope_difference <- beta_negative - beta_positive  # equals beta_2-hat

# Inference for beta_2 (classical OLS).
beta2_summary <- summary(model_asymmetric)$coefficients["interaction", ]
beta2_ci <- confint(model_asymmetric)["interaction", ]

# Partial F-test comparing the nested models (equivalent to the t-test).
nested_test <- anova(model_simple, model_asymmetric)

n_negative <- sum(data$negative)
n_nonnegative <- nrow(data) - n_negative
```

```{r}
#| label: hac-inference
#| include: false

# Primary inference: Newey-West HAC standard errors.
hac_lag <- 6
z_crit <- qnorm(0.975)

# One helper so every HAC calculation uses the same settings:
# Bartlett weights (NeweyWest default), fixed maximum lag,
# no prewhitening, no small-sample adjustment.
hac_vcov <- function(model, lag) {
  NeweyWest(model, lag = lag, prewhite = FALSE, adjust = FALSE)
}

vcov_hac <- hac_vcov(model_asymmetric, hac_lag)

beta2_hat <- unname(coef(model_asymmetric)["interaction"])

# Robust z-test and 95% CI for beta_2 (normal reference distribution).
beta2_hac_test <- coeftest(
  model_asymmetric, vcov. = vcov_hac, df = Inf
)["interaction", ]

beta2_hac_ci <- coefci(
  model_asymmetric, vcov. = vcov_hac, df = Inf
)["interaction", ]
```

## 1. Introduction

### Question and Motivation

Suppose the stock market rises by 5% in a given month and the healthcare industry rises by 3%. Would we expect healthcare stocks to respond with the same sensitivity if the market instead declined by 5%? A standard linear model of market sensitivity assumes that an industry's response remains constant regardless of whether the market rises or falls. However, there are reasons to question whether this assumption holds in practice. 

Behavioral economics provides one possible explanation for asymmetric responses. Under the principle of loss aversion, investors may react more strongly to losses than to equivalent gains, potentially influencing how stock prices respond to negative market conditions. Industry characteristics may also play a role. Healthcare, for example, is often considered a defensive industry because demand for medications, medical procedures, and other healthcare services tends to persist during economic downturns. As a result, healthcare stocks may be somewhat insulated from broader market declines. However, this does not necessarily mean that healthcare's sensitivity to market movements differs between gains and losses.

In financial economics, an industry's market sensitivity is commonly measured using its *beta*, the slope from a regression of industry excess returns on market excess returns. Excess return refers to an asset's return above the risk-free rate. The standard model assumes a single beta, regardless of market direction. Allowing different slopes for positive and negative market excess returns gives us a way to investigate potential asymmetry.

**Our primary research question is whether the healthcare industry's sensitivity to market movements differs between periods of positive and negative market excess returns.** Our goal is to estimate and test this difference, rather than predict future returns.

### Data

We obtain monthly financial data from the [Kenneth R. French Data Library](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/data_library.html), combining two publicly available datasets: the *Five Industry Portfolios* and the *Fama–French Research Data Factors*. Both datasets are constructed using stock return data from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP), covering eligible U.S. stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), American Stock Exchange (AMEX), and NASDAQ.

The *Five Industry Portfolios* dataset provides monthly value-weighted returns for five broad industry groups: consumer, manufacturing, technology, healthcare, and other. Stocks are assigned to these portfolios based on their four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes, using classifications from Compustat or CRSP. Portfolio assignments are updated annually in June, and returns are calculated for the following July through June. Within each portfolio, returns are weighted by market capitalization, meaning larger companies contribute more heavily to the portfolio's performance. Our primary focus is the healthcare portfolio, which includes companies involved in healthcare services, pharmaceuticals, and medical equipment.

The *Fama–French Research Data Factors* dataset provides monthly market excess returns (market) and the risk-free rate (RF). The market return is calculated as the value-weighted return of eligible U.S. common stocks in the CRSP database, representing a broader equity market than the S&P 500 alone. Market excess return is obtained by subtracting the one-month U.S. Treasury bill return from this market portfolio return. The risk-free rate is based on data from Ibbotson Associates through May 2024 and the ICE BofA US 1-Month Treasury Bill Index beginning in June 2024.

Our primary response variable is healthcare excess return, defined as the healthcare portfolio return minus the risk-free rate (healthcare). Our explanatory variable is market excess return (market). To examine whether healthcare responds differently to market gains and losses, we construct an indicator equal to one when market excess return is negative and zero otherwise, along with an interaction between the indicator and market excess return. All returns are measured in percentage points.

Our analysis sample contains `r nrow(data)` monthly observations from `r format(min(data$date), "%B %Y")` through `r format(max(data$date), "%B %Y")`, of which `r n_negative` months had negative market excess returns and `r n_nonnegative` had nonnegative ones. We restrict the sample to January 2000 onward to focus on relatively recent financial market conditions while retaining sufficient observations for estimation and hypothesis testing.

To prepare the data, we extract monthly value-weighted industry returns and monthly market factors, excluding annual summaries. The datasets were then merged by their year-month identifiers. We then checked for missing values and verified that the sample contains consecutive monthly observations without gaps or duplicate dates. Automated validation checks also confirm chronological consistency and the correct construction of excess returns and interaction variables.

### Setting of Our Conclusions

Our conclusions concern the relationship between monthly excess returns on value-weighted U.S. industry portfolios and the broader U.S. equity market from January 2000 through September 2026. Our analysis focuses on the healthcare portfolio. Because these portfolios consist of publicly traded U.S. stocks and are weighted by market capitalization, our findings primarily characterize the behavior of broad industry portfolios rather than individual companies. We do not claim that these relationships extend to international markets, daily returns, or future periods. Furthermore, our analysis identifies statistical associations between contemporaneous market and industry returns and does not establish causality or provide evidence of predictive performance.

## 2. Methods

### Models

Let $Y_t$ denote healthcare excess return and $X_t$ denote market excess return in month $t$, both measured in percent. We first fit a single-slope benchmark by ordinary least squares (OLS):
$$
Y_t = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 X_t + u_t.
$$ {#eq-simple}
In this model, a one-percentage-point increase in market excess return is associated with an $\alpha_1$-percentage-point change in fitted healthcare excess return. The model uses the same slope across the full range of market returns.

To allow market sensitivity to differ between negative and nonnegative months, we define $D_t = \mathbf{1}(X_t < 0)$ and fit
$$
Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_t + \beta_2 X_t D_t + \varepsilon_t.
$$ {#eq-asymmetric}
When $X_t \geq 0$, the interaction is zero and the slope is $\beta_1$. When $X_t < 0$, the interaction equals $X_t$ and the slope is $\beta_1 + \beta_2$. Both segments have the fitted value $\beta_0$ at $X_t = 0$, so the regression is continuous at zero. We use a common intercept because we expect the fitted healthcare excess return to change continuously as market excess return crosses zero. Months just below and just above zero have nearly identical market excess returns, and we have no specific reason to expect an abrupt shift in fitted healthcare returns at that boundary.

### Hypothesis Test and Estimation

Our parameter of interest is the negative-market slope minus the nonnegative-market slope,
$$
(\beta_1 + \beta_2) - \beta_1 = \beta_2.
$$
We test $H_0: \beta_2 = 0$ against $H_A: \beta_2 \neq 0$. Under the null, the piecewise model (@eq-asymmetric) reduces to the single-slope model (@eq-simple). Under the conventional OLS assumptions, the two-sided $t$-test for $\beta_2$ is equivalent to the partial $F$-test comparing the two models ($F = t^2$). We report point estimates and 95% confidence intervals for $\alpha_1$, $\beta_1$, $\beta_1 + \beta_2$, and $\beta_2$.

### Assumptions and Assessing Uncertainty

Let $\mathbf X$ denote the observed series of market excess returns. Conventional OLS standard errors assume that $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_t \mid \mathbf X) = \sigma^2$ for every month and that $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_t, \varepsilon_s \mid \mathbf X) = 0$ for distinct months $t$ and $s$. Constant variance means that the spread of healthcare returns around the fitted relationship is the same across months. This assumption may be restrictive because the market return captures only part of what moves the healthcare portfolio; for example, an unexpectedly successful trial or rejected drug application could move pharmaceutical or biotech stocks. During periods of heightened uncertainty, the deviations from the fitted relationship may be larger and may stay large for several months.

We plot residuals against fitted values to check whether their spread changes with the fitted return. We also examine the autocorrelations of raw and squared residuals. Raw residuals help detect whether positive or negative deviations persist. Squared residuals help detect whether large deviations tend to occur near one another in time. As supplemental checks, we use a studentized Breusch–Pagan test for variance related to the model regressors and a Breusch–Godfrey test for serial correlation through six months.

For $\beta_2$, we report the OLS estimate, a 95% confidence interval, and a two-sided $p$-value using Newey–West heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) standard errors. We use Bartlett weights and a maximum lag of six months, giving nearer months more weight in estimating the covariance. Six months is slightly longer than the common rule-of-thumb lag $\lfloor 4(T/100)^{2/9} \rfloor =$ `r floor(4 * (nrow(data) / 100)^(2/9))` for our $T =$ `r nrow(data)` months, and allows deviations to remain related for up to half a year. HAC inference relies on large-sample approximations rather than normally distributed errors, so we compare the HAC $z$-statistic with the standard normal distribution. We compare the primary result with conventional OLS inference and with HAC calculations using maximum lags of 0, 3, and 12 months.

### Sensitivity Analyses

To assess influence, we rank months by the absolute DFBETAS for $\beta_2$, which measures the standardized change in the estimated slope difference when a month is omitted. We refit the same model after omitting each of the three highest-ranked months individually and then all three together, using the same HAC standard errors as the primary analysis. High influence alone does not indicate a data error: these months are real market events, so the full sample remains the basis for the primary result, and the refits show only how much our conclusion depends on them.

## 3. Results

### Fitted OLS Models

@fig-healthcare plots monthly healthcare excess returns against market excess returns, together with the fitted piecewise model (@eq-asymmetric).

```{r}
#| label: fig-healthcare
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Healthcare excess returns versus market excess returns. The lines are fitted values from the piecewise model (@eq-asymmetric), whose two segments share an intercept and meet at zero."
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 2.65
#| fig-align: center

plot_data <- data.frame(
  market = seq(min(data$market), max(data$market), length.out = 300)
)
plot_data$interaction <- plot_data$market * (plot_data$market < 0)
plot_data$fitted <- predict(model_asymmetric, newdata = plot_data)
plot_data$direction <- ifelse(
  plot_data$market < 0,
  "Negative market excess return",
  "Nonnegative market excess return"
)

ggplot(data, aes(x = market, y = health)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, color = "gray45", size = 1.2) +
  geom_line(
    data = plot_data,
    aes(x = market, y = fitted, color = direction),
    linewidth = 1,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(
    x = "Market excess return (%)",
    y = "Healthcare excess return (%)",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    plot.margin = margin(2, 2, 2, 2)
  )
```

The single-slope benchmark gives $\hat\alpha_1 =$ `r sprintf("%.2f", coef(model_simple)["market"])`. In the piecewise model, the estimated slopes are `r sprintf("%.2f", beta_positive)` for nonnegative market excess returns and `r sprintf("%.2f", beta_negative)` for negative market excess returns. Both are below one, suggesting that healthcare returns are generally less sensitive to market movements than a portfolio with a beta of one. The two slopes are also similar: the estimated difference is $\hat\beta_2 =$ `r sprintf("%.3f", slope_difference)`, and allowing separate slopes barely changes the fit ($R^2 =$ `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(model_simple)$r.squared)` for @eq-simple and `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(model_asymmetric)$r.squared)` for @eq-asymmetric).

Under conventional OLS inference, the 95% confidence interval for $\beta_2$ is `r sprintf("%.3f", beta2_ci[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", beta2_ci[2])` ($t =$ `r sprintf("%.2f", beta2_summary["t value"])`, $p =$ `r format.pval(beta2_summary["Pr(>|t|)"], digits = 2)`; equivalently, the partial $F$-test gives $F =$ `r sprintf("%.2f", nested_test$F[2])`). These standard errors assume constant error variance and uncorrelated errors, which we check next.

### Checking the OLS Assumptions

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the piecewise model. (a) Residuals against fitted values. (b) Residuals over time. (c) Autocorrelation of residuals. (d) Autocorrelation of squared residuals. Dashed blue lines mark approximate 95% bounds under no autocorrelation."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

diag_data <- data |>
  mutate(
    fitted = fitted(model_asymmetric),
    resid = resid(model_asymmetric)
  )

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex = 0.75)

# Residuals vs. fitted: does the spread change with the fitted return?
plot(diag_data$fitted, diag_data$resid,
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "(a) Residuals vs. fitted", pch = 16, col = "gray40")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Residuals over time: are there periods of larger deviations?
plot(diag_data$date, diag_data$resid, type = "l",
     xlab = "Month", ylab = "Residuals", main = "(b) Residuals over time")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# ACF of raw residuals: do positive or negative deviations persist?
acf(diag_data$resid, lag.max = 24, main = "")
title("(c) ACF of residuals", line = 0.8)

# ACF of squared residuals: do large deviations cluster in time?
acf(diag_data$resid^2, lag.max = 24, main = "")
title("(d) ACF of squared residuals", line = 0.8)
```

```{r}
#| label: residual-tests
#| include: false

bp_test <- bptest(model_asymmetric)             # studentized Breusch-Pagan
bg_test <- bgtest(model_asymmetric, order = 6)  # Breusch-Godfrey, 6 lags

# Residual standard deviation by calendar year, to describe panel (b).
resid_sd_by_year <- tapply(
  resid(model_asymmetric), format(data$date, "%Y"), sd
)
```

@fig-diagnostics shows the residual checks. Panel (a) shows no strong funnel shape against the fitted values, but panel (b) shows that the size of the deviations changes over time: the residual standard deviation is about `r sprintf("%.1f", resid_sd_by_year["2000"])` percentage points in 2000 and `r sprintf("%.1f", resid_sd_by_year["2025"])` in 2025, compared with roughly 2 to 3 in most other years. Panel (c) shows little autocorrelation in the raw residuals, so the direction of a deviation does not persist from month to month. Panel (d), however, shows positive autocorrelation in the squared residuals at several lags up to about one year, so large deviations tend to occur near one another in time.

The supplemental tests point the same way. The studentized Breusch–Pagan test gives $BP =$ `r sprintf("%.2f", bp_test$statistic)` on `r bp_test$parameter` degrees of freedom ($p =$ `r format.pval(bp_test$p.value, digits = 2)`), modest evidence that the residual variance is related to the regressors. The Breusch–Godfrey test through six lags gives $LM =$ `r sprintf("%.2f", bg_test$statistic)` ($p =$ `r format.pval(bg_test$p.value, digits = 2)`), so it does not detect correlation in the residuals themselves. Together, the checks suggest that the errors do not have constant variance and that their magnitudes are dependent over time. Conventional OLS standard errors ignore both features and may understate the uncertainty in $\hat\beta_2$.

### Robust Inference for the Slope Difference

We therefore base inference on Newey–West HAC standard errors. @tbl-models reports the estimated slopes with HAC standard errors and confidence intervals.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated slopes with Newey-West HAC standard errors (Bartlett weights, maximum lag 6) and 95% confidence intervals."

c_neg <- c(0, 1, 1)  # picks out beta_1 + beta_2
se_hac <- sqrt(diag(vcov_hac))
se_negative_hac <- sqrt(drop(t(c_neg) %*% vcov_hac %*% c_neg))
se_simple_hac <- sqrt(hac_vcov(model_simple, hac_lag)["market", "market"])

estimates <- c(
  coef(model_simple)["market"],
  beta_positive,
  beta_negative,
  beta2_hat
)
ses <- c(se_simple_hac, se_hac["market"], se_negative_hac, se_hac["interaction"])

model_table <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Single slope, $\\alpha_1$",
    "Nonnegative-market slope, $\\beta_1$",
    "Negative-market slope, $\\beta_1 + \\beta_2$",
    "Difference, $\\beta_2$"
  ),
  Estimate = unname(estimates),
  `HAC SE` = unname(ses),
  `CI lower` = unname(estimates - z_crit * ses),
  `CI upper` = unname(estimates + z_crit * ses),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(model_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE)
```

The estimated difference in slopes is $\hat\beta_2 =$ `r sprintf("%.3f", beta2_hat)` (95% HAC CI `r sprintf("%.3f", beta2_hac_ci[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", beta2_hac_ci[2])`; $z =$ `r sprintf("%.2f", beta2_hac_test["z value"])`, $p =$ `r format.pval(beta2_hac_test["Pr(>|z|)"], digits = 2)`). The interval contains zero, so we do not reject $H_0: \beta_2 = 0$. This does not show that the two sensitivities are equal: the data are consistent with a negative-market slope anywhere from about `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(beta2_hac_ci[1]))` lower to `r sprintf("%.2f", beta2_hac_ci[2])` higher than the nonnegative-market slope.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lag-comparison
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Inference for $\\beta_2$ under conventional OLS and Newey-West HAC standard errors with maximum lags of 0, 3, 6 (primary), and 12 months. The point estimate is the same in every row. SE ratio is each standard error divided by the OLS standard error."

se_ols <- sqrt(vcov(model_asymmetric)["interaction", "interaction"])
df_ols <- df.residual(model_asymmetric)

summarize_beta2 <- function(method, se, crit, p) {
  data.frame(
    Method = method,
    SE = se,
    `CI lower` = beta2_hat - crit * se,
    `CI upper` = beta2_hat + crit * se,
    `p-value` = p,
    `SE ratio` = se / se_ols,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

# Conventional OLS: t reference distribution with n - 3 df.
ols_row <- summarize_beta2(
  "Conventional OLS", se_ols,
  crit = qt(0.975, df_ols),
  p = 2 * pt(-abs(beta2_hat / se_ols), df_ols)
)

# HAC at each lag: normal reference distribution.
hac_lags <- c(0, 3, 6, 12)
hac_rows <- lapply(hac_lags, function(lag) {
  se <- sqrt(hac_vcov(model_asymmetric, lag)["interaction", "interaction"])
  label <- paste0("HAC, lag ", lag, if (lag == hac_lag) " (primary)" else "")
  summarize_beta2(label, se, crit = z_crit, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(beta2_hat / se)))
})

lag_table <- rbind(ols_row, do.call(rbind, hac_rows))

# SE ratios for the text (rows 2-5 are the HAC lags, in order).
se_ratio <- setNames(lag_table$`SE ratio`[-1], hac_lags)

lag_table$`p-value` <- format.pval(lag_table$`p-value`, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)

knitr::kable(lag_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

@tbl-lag-comparison shows how much the choice of standard error matters. The primary HAC standard error is `r sprintf("%.2f", se_ratio["6"])` times the conventional OLS standard error, and the ratio grows from `r sprintf("%.2f", se_ratio["0"])` with no lags to `r sprintf("%.2f", se_ratio["12"])` with twelve. Conventional OLS therefore overstates the precision of $\hat\beta_2$, but every interval contains zero, so the conclusion does not depend on the lag choice.

### Sensitivity to Influential Months

```{r}
#| label: influence
#| include: false

dfbetas_beta2 <- dfbetas(model_asymmetric)[, "interaction"]
top_idx <- order(abs(dfbetas_beta2), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]

influential_months <- data.frame(
  Month = format(data$date[top_idx], "%B %Y"),
  market = data$market[top_idx],
  health = data$health[top_idx],
  dfbetas = dfbetas_beta2[top_idx]
)

refit_row <- function(label, drop_idx = integer(0)) {
  fit_data <- if (length(drop_idx) > 0) data[-drop_idx, ] else data
  fit <- lm(health ~ market + interaction, data = fit_data)
  est <- unname(coef(fit)["interaction"])
  se <- sqrt(hac_vcov(fit, hac_lag)["interaction", "interaction"])
  data.frame(
    Sample = label,
    Months = nobs(fit),
    Estimate = est,
    `HAC SE` = se,
    `CI lower` = est - z_crit * se,
    `CI upper` = est + z_crit * se,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

influence_table <- rbind(
  refit_row("Full sample"),
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(top_idx), function(i) {
    refit_row(paste("Omit", influential_months$Month[i]), top_idx[i])
  })),
  refit_row("Omit all three", top_idx)
)

refit_estimates <- influence_table$Estimate[-1]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-influence
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of $\\hat\\beta_2$ to the three months with the largest absolute DFBETAS. Intervals use HAC standard errors (maximum lag 6)."

knitr::kable(influence_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The three most influential months for $\hat\beta_2$ are `r paste(influential_months$Month, collapse = ", ")`, with DFBETAS of `r paste(sprintf("%.2f", influential_months$dfbetas), collapse = ", ")`. All three had large positive market excess returns (`r paste(sprintf("%.1f", influential_months$market), collapse = ", ")` percent). Because $\beta_2$ is the difference between the two slopes, months on the nonnegative side influence it through $\hat\beta_1$. Omitting these months moves $\hat\beta_2$ to between `r sprintf("%.3f", min(refit_estimates))` and `r sprintf("%.3f", max(refit_estimates))` (@tbl-influence), and every interval still contains zero.
